པོ་དཔལ་བས་བརྗེད་བྱང་དུ་མཛད་པ་ ༈ འཁྲིད་ཡིད་མཁའི་སྤྱོད་བགྲོད་པའི་ཉེ་ལམ་ཚར་ཆེན་གྱི་གསུང་ལ་འཇམ་དབྱངས་མཁྱེན་བརྩེའི་དབང་ཕྱུག་གིས་ཟིན་བྲིས་མཛད་པ་
<leaf-break/>
མཛད་པ་། ༈ ལུས་དཀྱིལ་སྙན་རྒྱུད་ཚར་ཆེན་གྱིས་མཛད་པ་། ༈ ཡང་བླ་མའི་རྣལ་འབྱོར་དང་མཁའ་སྤྱོད་སྒྲུབ་པའི་ཡིག་ཆུང་ས་སྐྱ་པའི་མན་ངག་ ༈ ཕྱག་རྒྱ་ཆེན་པོ་
དབུ་མར་འཇུག་པའི་ཡིག་རྙིང་། ༈ རྩ་དབུ་མའི་རྒྱུན་གྱི་ཉམས་ལེན་གསང་ཆེན་བཅུད་ཀྱི་ཐིག་ལེ་ཚར་པ་རྡོ་རྗེ་འཆང་གིས་མཛད་པ་ ༈ མཁའ་སྤྱོད་མའི་ཞལ་ཤེས་དབང་
བཞི་ལུས་སྒྲིགས་ཀྱི་ཡིག་ཆུང་བླ་མའི་གསུང་། ༈ ཡང་དབང་(ཨེ་)བཞི་ལུས་སྒྲིགས་མཁའ་སྤྱོད་སྒྲུབ་པ་འཕོ་བའི་སྐབས་སྒོ་དགག་པ་གསུམ་གྱི་(ཨི་དྷི་)ཞལ་ཤེས་རྒྱུད་ལས་གསལ་
བར་འབྱུང་བ་ ༈ ཧེ་རུ་ཀ་ཡབ་ཡུམ་དང་ཡུམ་རྐྱང་ལ་བརྟེན་པའི་འཕོ་བ་གསེར་ཆོ་ལོ་ཙཱ་བའི་མན་ངག་པ་ཆེན་གྱིས་མཛད་པ་ ༈ དེའི་གསལ་བྱེད་ཡབ་དང་མཐུན་མོང་
བ་དང་ཡུམ་གྱིས་ཐུན་མོང་མ་ཡིན་པ་ཚར་པ་རྡོ་རྗེ་འཆང་གིས་བཛད་པ་ ༈ ཡང་སྔ་མ་དང་འདྲ་མིན་གང་གི་ཁྱོད་ཞབས་མ་ལོ་ཙཱ་བའི་གསེར་ཆོས་ ༈ མཁའ་སྤྱོད་
སྒྲུབ་པའི་གསེར་ཆོས་ཤིན་ཏུ་ཟབ་པའི་ཚིག་རྒྱུད་མ་ཚར་པ་རྡོ་རྗེ་འཆང་གིས་ཕན་ཡུལ་ཨཽ་ཌི་ཡ་ནའི་གཞིས་གར་མཛད་པ་ ༈ མཁའ་སྤྱོད་ཞལ་བཟང་བལྟ་བའི་སྨོན་
<leaf-break/>
པ་། ༈ རྒྱལ་ཆེན་ཨིནྚ་བྷུ་ཏིས་ལེགས་པར་བཀྲལ་བ་ཨིནྚ་མཁའ་སྤྱོད་དམ་ཕག་མོ་ཞལ་གཉིས་མར་གྲགས་པའི་ཆོས་སྐོར་ལ་། མི་དབང་ཆོས་གསུམ་དུ་གྲགས་
པའི་དང་པོ་ རྡོ་རྗེ་རྣམ་འབྱོར་མའི་སྒྲུབ་ཐབས་ཨྱོན་གྱི་སློབ་དཔོན་ཆེན་པོ་མི་དབང་ཨིནྚ་བྷུ་ཏིས་མཛད་པ་རྒྱ་གར་གྱི་མཁན་པོ་དཔལ་ནཱ་ལན་པ་དང་། ལོ་ཙཱ་བ་པྲཛྙཱ་ཀཱིརྟིས་
བསྒྱུར་བ་ གཉིས་པ་དེས་མཁའ་འགྲོ་རྒྱ་མཚོའི་རྒྱུད་ལ་རྟེན་ནས་མཛད་པའི་སྔཌ་ཀྱི་དེ་ཁོ་ན་ཉིད་(དྷཱི)་རང་བྱིན་གྱིས་རློབ་པའི་རིམ་པ་སློབ་མ་ཡེ་ཤེས་རྡོ་རྗེས་བསྒྱུར་བ་ ༈ གསུམ་
པ་ལས་བཅུ་ཞེས་པ་བསྙེན་པའི་ཆོ་ག་ གཞན་དོན་དུ་སློབ་མ་རྗེས་སུ་བཟུང་བ་ ཚེས་བཅུ་དང་འབྲེལ་བའི་ཚོགས་(དྷཱི)་མཆོད་བདག་གཞན་གཉིས་ཀ་དང་འབྲེལ་བ་གཞོན་ནུ་
མའི་མཆོད་པ་ ༈ གནས་སྐབས་ཐམས་ཅད་དང་འབྲེལ་བ་གཏོར་མའི་ཆོ་ག་ དམན་པའི་དུར་ཁྲོད་དང་འབྲེལ་བ་སྦྱིན་སྲེག་གི་ཆོ་ག་ བུ་ཆུང་གསར་བུ་ལ་ཕན་འདོགས་པ་
བསྲུང་བའི་འཁོར་ལོ་ རྩུབ་ལས་བདུག་པ་ཅན་ཚར་གཅོད་པ་སུམྦྷ་ནའི་ཆོ་ག་ བསྒོམ་པས་ཕྱིར་བཟློག་པ་(༩)དང་ བྲིས་པས་ཕྱིར་བཟློག་པ་རྣམས་བླ་མ་བྷ་རེནྡྲ་རུ་རྩེས་མཛད་

A concise daily practice <note>Tibetan: rgyun gyi nyams len</note> recorded as a reminder by Tenzin Nyida Zangpo. The ritual for the offering cake <note>Tibetan: gtor chog</note> at the end of the practice composed by the Great Tsarchen Dorje Chang. The explanation of the Sadhana for the Sky-Farer Varahi in the generation stage, composed by Lord Nyida Senge. Also, the explanation of the eleven applications composed by Lord Jampa Cholek. Also, the explanation of Vajrayogini composed by Ngawang Nyida Zangpo. Regarding the cycle of blessings: The ritual for entering the mandala and receiving the empowerment of Vajrayogini, composed by Phagpa Rinchen. The text for the method of bestowing the blessing composed by Lord Sangye Pelzang. Also, the ritual for the blessing according to the speech of Dorje Chang Anantabhadra, as recorded by Prajnabhadra. The ritual for accomplishing the cinnabar mandala, making offerings, entering, and receiving the empowerment, a specialty for achieving the Sky-Farer, composed by the Tsarpa Dharma Lord. By Gunru Sherab Zangpo. Also, the ritual for the blessing "Meaningful to Behold," composed by Namkha Pelzang of Ewam Tartse. The ritual for the blessing that directly demonstrates the nature of reality, composed by Ngawang Kunga Sonam of the glorious Sakya tradition. The ritual for the blessing as recorded from the speech of Dorje Chang Anantabhadra, composed by Prajnabhadra.

<leaf-break/>

Composed by <note>unclear</note>. Regarding the cycle of teachings in the Dzongchungpa tradition: Making the deity pleased through retreat based on the practice of the eleven yogas. The supplementary ritual for the offering cake. Benefiting others through the student's initiation together with the feast offering. The text for the blessing that accepts the student. Supplementary practice of the cinnabar mandala. The peaceful fire offering. The butter lamp fire offering. The ritual of purification. The secret instructions on the chakra. The collected rituals for the tenth day festival, known as the "Treasury of Secret Instructions," composed by the Mantra-Holder Zungpa. Regarding the cycle of the instructional manuals for liberation, specifically the two cycles of the Great Central Channel: First, the manual for the central channel taken from the Great Seal collection of the Great Venerable One, written by Konchog Gyaltsen of the Chakrasamvara tradition. The notes on the generation and completion stages of Naro Sky-Farer, recorded as a reminder by Zangpo Pel, the direct student of Palden Gyalpo. The "Short Path for Journeying to the Sky-Farer Realm," a manual of instruction based on the speech of Tsarchen, recorded as notes by Jamyang Khyentse Wangchuk.

<leaf-break/>

Composed by <note>unclear</note>. The oral lineage of the body mandala composed by Tsarchen. Also, the minor text for the Guru Yoga and the Sky-Farer accomplishment, a secret instruction of the Sakyapas. An old manuscript on the entry of the Great Seal into the Middle Way. "The Essence-Drop of the Great Secret," a practice for the flow of the central channel, composed by Tsarpa Dorje Chang. A minor text on the body arrangement of the four empowerments, the secret instruction of the Sky-Farer, according to the Guru's speech. Also, the secret instruction from the Tantras regarding the three doors for blocking at the time of the transference of consciousness in the Sky-Farer achievement and the four empowerments. The "Golden Dharma" <note>Tibetan: gser chos</note> transference of consciousness based on Heruka Father-Mother and the solitary Mother, composed by the Great Lotsawa. The clarification of this, both the common practice with the Father and the uncommon practice with the Mother, composed by Tsarpa Dorje Chang. Also, the Golden Dharma of Ma Lotsawa, whether identical or different from the previous. The highly profound verse-lineage of the Golden Dharma for achieving the Sky-Farer, composed by Tsarpa Dorje Chang at the estate of Uddiyana in Phanyul. A prayer to behold the beautiful face of the Sky-Farer.

<leaf-break/>

Well-explained by the Great King Indrabhuti. Regarding the cycle of teachings known as "Indra's Sky-Farer" or the "Two-Faced Varahi": The first of the "Three Cycles of the Lord of Men," the Sadhana of Vajrayogini, composed by the great master of Uddiyana, the Lord of Men Indrabhuti, and translated by the Indian scholar Pal Nalanda and the translator Prajnakirti. Second, the stages of the self-blessing of the reality of mantra, composed by him based on the Dakini Ocean Tantra <note>Dakarnava Tantra</note>, translated by the student Yeshe Dorje. Third, the "Ten Activities": the ritual for retreat; the acceptance of the student for the sake of others; the feast offering related to the tenth day festival; the "Offering of the Youthful Maiden" which relates to both oneself and others; the ritual of the offering cake related to all occasions; the ritual of the fire offering related to the cemetery; the protective wheel for benefiting young children; the ritual of Sumbhani for subduing harmful spirits during harsh activities; the methods for reversing through meditation and reversing through drawings, composed by Lama Barendra Rutse.

གནས་ཤས་ཆེ་ན་ལྷར་ལྡང་། གསལ་བ་དང་བདེ་ཤས་ཆེ་ན་མཉམ་པར་བཞག། གསལ་བ་དང་བདེ་ཤས་ཚེ་ན་སྟོང་པར་བཞག། ལྷར་ལྡང་བ་ནི་སྔར་ལྟར་རྗེ་བཙུན་མ་ལ་ཕྱག་མཚན་མེད་པའི་སྐུར་ལྡང་ངོ་།། བཅུ་གཅིག་པ་སྤྱོད་ལམ་གྱི་

The wind below moves, the fire blazes, boiling the substances, which melt and are visualized as a great ocean of nectar. Collect the leftovers, and with the "blazing gesture" and the sound <term>Phem</term>, spray common beer from the mouth. With the <term>Akaro</term> mantra, give it to the elemental spirits residing outside three times. ཞལ་ཤེས་ཆོག་བརྒྱུད་གསེར་གྱི་མཎྜལ་དང་བཅས་པ་ཞུས་ཏེ་ཉམས་སུ་བླངས་ན། མཁའ་སྤྱོད་གྲུབ་པའི་ཐབས་ཀྱི་གཙོ་བོ་ནི་འདི་ཡིན་གསུངས་པས། སྙིང་གི་དཀྱིལ་དུ་སྦ་བར་བྱའོ། དེ་གཉིས་གང་རུང་གི་གོ་ནས་
(༧)མི་གསལ་ན་མི་གསལ་ཏེ་འཕྲོ་བཅད།

...should be done until midnight. On the twenty-fourth, for two-thirds of the night. On the twenty-fifth, recite throughout the entire night. Just as dawn breaks, take out the <term>sindura</term> and carry it home, placing it in the center of the mandala. Perform elaborate outer offerings and the Self-Entry. When the sun rises, the companion is no longer needed. Ideally, enter alone in the attire of a <term>kusali</term> <gloss>simple mendicant</gloss>. Reveal the "Bliss-Whirl" <note>design</note> from the base of the <term>sindura</term> and press it against your forehead, then conceal the <term>sindura</term> under your left armpit where no one can see. Carrying the staff blessed by the recitations, wander through all the outskirts. Go to places where many women gather, like an archery range. With the firm pride of Vajra Yogini, when you look at those women, the reflection of the "Bliss-Whirl" on your forehead will appear on one woman's forehead, like an image in a mirror. If it appears, she is the actual Vajra Yogini; without any doubt or hesitation, place her feet on your crown. Circling from the left...

<leaf-break/>

...is for those of the lowest faculties. Even they should practice with intense devotion without interruption. Specifically, at the time of death, Vajra Yogini will certainly accept them. However, the method for making it happen quickly is to practice the Yoga of Transference <term>powa</term>. Regarding this, whether it is the Transference of the Father and Mother in Union or the Transference of the Mother alone, whichever one prefers, one should seal the retreat strictly for at least seven days and practice. The crown of the head will swell, and signs like the oozing of pus, blood, or yellow fluid will occur. For that yogi, as signs of accomplishing Kechara, an individual rainbow tent will form over the practice house, a rain of flowers will fall, and an excellent fragrance will waft. Since such trustworthy signs occur, from then on, just do not forget it and if you meditate intensely, it is called the "Great Success of Transference." However, if it is too intense, there is a danger of it becoming "ashes" <note>premature death</note>; so do not be hasty, but put the practice into the vital points. When the time eventually arrives, it is the engagement with karma. Regarding that, the signs of death...

<leaf-break/>

This summary of whatever could be held in mind was written to cut through misconceptions regarding the elaborate explanation of the Generation Stage. Regarding the engagement of mental focus in the practice of the decided meaning: of the two—Generation Stage and Completion Stage—the first is as follows. By the condition of dissolving the Guru into oneself, all phenomena dissolve into the Clear Light. Within that state, from the syllable <term>E</term> in one's heart until the <term>SHUDDHO HAM</term> mantra, meditate in a forceful and swift manner without being interrupted by other thoughts. Perform the verbal recitation, the mental recitation, and at the end of meditating on the Completion Stage as an ancillary, first hold the mind on the pride of thinking, "I am not an ordinary person, I am the actual Vajra Yogini." Then, hold the mind on the general form: red in color, one face, two arms, complete with handheld implements, residing in the center of a blazing fire. Then, hold the mind on the central eye: its center is black, its edges white, its base a flickering red, looking as if the left eye is looking upward.

<leaf-break/>

...the two legs, the anklets, the girdle at the waist. From the shoulders to the thighs, the hanging necklace of fifty dry skulls strung together with human hair. The blazing fire of pristine awareness. Hold the mind on these in sequence. From the central eye to the mountain of fire, if each one is vivid, stop the progression while it remains vivid. Since one is not separated from the key point called "extracting the poison of conceptual thought," practice until the sign of "touching" is obtained. Likewise, from the central deity of the body mandala to the retinue, for each one, hold the mind on everything from the central eye to the fire mountain. If one wishes to (...) from that session, then according to the general "Inconceivable" <note>Yoga</note> that arises from the sequence of the <term>Abhisamaya</term> <gloss>Clear Realization</gloss>, and the superior "Uncommon Inconceivable" which accomplishes Kechara through the three oral instructions, if one receives and practices the oral instructions along with the Golden Mandala of the lineage, it is said that this is the main method for accomplishing Kechara. Thus, hide it in the center of your heart. If it is not clear from either of those perspectives, stop the progression while it remains unclear.

མཐིང་པ་སྐུ་མཆེད་ལ་གནང་བའི་གདམས་པ་ ཟབ་ཤེས་བསྐྱེད་རིམ་དང་ རྫོགས་རིམ་ཆ་ལག་དང་བཅས་པ་རྣམས་ཡོད་པ་ལས་བསྐྱེད་
རིམ་ནཱ་རོ་མཁའ་སྤྱོད་རྣལ་འབྱོར་བཅུ་གཅིག་གི་བསྒོམ་པའི་ཚུལ་ནི་ ཇོ་བོ་ནཱ་རོ་པས་རྒྱ་གཞུང་དང་ ཚད་མེད་དང་པོར་གསུང་ནའང་ཤེས་
ལེན་གོ་རིམ་གྱི་དབང་དུ་བྱས་ནས་། འདི་ལྟར་ཡིན་ཏེ་ ཉལ་དང་ལྡང་དང་བདུད་རྩི་མྱང་། ཚད་མེད་བླ་མ་བདག་ལྷར་བསྐྱེད་། འགྲོ་བ་དག་
<leaf-break/>
ནི་ བསྐྱེད་རིམ་གྱི་ངང་ལ་ཉལ་བ་ཡིན་ན་རྣལ་འབྱོར་མ་རྒྱན་དང་ཕྱག་མཚན་སྤངས་པའི་སྐུར་། ནམ་མཁར་ཌ་མ་རུའི་སྒྲ་དང་ཨོཾ་གསུཾ་
མ་གྲགས་པས་རྐྱེན་བྱས་ནས་ལྡང་། བསམ་མི་ཁྱབ་ལྟར་ན་ ཆུ་ལས་ཐ་ལྡང་གི་ཚུལ་དུ་རྣལ་འབྱོར་མར་ལྡང་ངོ་ བདུད་རྩི་མྱང་བ་ནི་
ཆང་ལ་བདུད་རྩི་རིལ་བུ་བཏབ་ལ་སྙིང་ཁའི་ཐེ་མཆོད་པའི་བསམ་པས་མྱང་བར་བྱའོ་། ཚད་མེད་ཀྱི་རྣལ་འབྱོར་ནི་ སེམས་བསྐྱེད་ལ་ཚད་
མེད་ཚང་བས་ལོགས་སུ་མི་དགོས་སོ་། བླ་མའི་རྣལ་འབྱོར་ནི་ བླ་མ་རྡོ་རྗེ་ཆོས་ཀྱི་རྣམ་པར་བསྒོམ་ལ་གསོལ་བ་གདབ་པ་ལྷཾ་
ན་། བདག་ལྷར་བསྐྱེད་པ་ནི་ གཞན་དཀྱུས་ལྟར་ལ་བེ་ཡིག་སྔཌ་ཕྲེང་དང་བཅས་པ་ལསྭ་འོད་འཕྲོས་ལུས་ནང་གང་བས་སྡིག་སྒྲིབ་སྦྱང་
<leaf-break/>
མཚན་སྤངས་པའི་ང་རྒྱལ་གྱིས་འཇུག་པའོ་། དེ་ལྟར་བཤད་པའི་བསྐྱེད་རིམ་སོགས་འདི་རྣམས་གཞན་ལས་ཁྱད་པར་དུ་འཕགས་པ་ཡིན་ཏེ་ རྣལ་འབྱོར་གསང་མཐའི་
མཐར་ཐུག་གི་སྨིན་གྲོལ་མ་ལུས་པ་འདིར་ལུས་པའི་ཕྱིར་རོ་། དེའང་སྨིན་བྱེད་དབང་བཞི་ཡིན་ལ་ དེ་འདིར་ལུས་ཏེ་ དེའང་ངག་བཟླས་བུམ་དབང་གི་ལམ་དུ་ངོ་སྤྲད་ ཡིད་
བཟླས་གསང་དབང་གི་ལམ་དུ་ངོ་སྤྲད ་དབང་གོང་མ་གཉིས་ཟུར་དུ་བསྟན་ཏེ་ངོ་སྤྲོད་པའོ་། དོི་བུམ་དབང་གི་ལམ་རྒྱས་པ་ནི་ བདེ་མཆོག་ཡོངས་རྫོགས་ཡིན་ལ་ དེ་ནི་
འདིར་ཚང་སྟེ་ ཡབ་ཀྱི་བསྐྱེད་རིམ་རྒྱས་པའི་ཆོས་འབྱུང་གཞལ་ཡས་ཁང་ནི་ འདིའི་ཆོས་འབྱུང་ཉིས་བརྩེགས་ཀྱི་རིམ་བཞིན་མཆོན་ དེའི་ནང་གི་ཟླ་བ་ནི་ བཅོམ་ལྡན་
འདས་ནས་རྡོ་རྗེ་སེམས་དཔའི་བར་གྱི་ལྷ་དཔའ་བོ་ཉེར་ལྔ་ འདིའི་ཆོས་འབྱུང་ཉིས་གཤེགས་ཀྱི་རིམ་བཞིན་མཆོན་དེའི་ནང་གི་ཟླ་བ་ནི་ བཅོལ་ལྡན་འདས་ནས་རྡོ་
རྗེ་སེམས་དཔའི་བར་གྱི་ལྷ་འབར་གྱི་ལྷ་དཔའ་བོ་ཉེར་ལྔ། དབུསྱི་བཾ་ལས་འབྱུང་བཞིའི་ས་བོན་ཚང་བ་ནི་ སྙིང་པོའི་རྣལ་འབྱོར་མ་བཞི་ བེཾ་གྱི་ཀླད་ཀོར་རྗེ་བཙུན་མ་ སྔགས་འཕྲེང་
<leaf-break/>
དབང་གོང་མ་གཉིས་ཟུར་དུབསྟན་པ་ནི་ ཆོས་འབྱུང་བེཾ་དང་བཅས་པ་གསང་གནས་སུ་བསྒོམ་པ་ལ་ ཆོས་འབྱུང་གི་མདུན་རྒྱབ་དོར་བའི་གྲྭ་བཞིར་ དགའ་བ་འཁྱིལ་པ་དེ་
གཡོན་དུ་གནས་པར་འཁོར་བར་བསམ་ལ་རླུང་ཁ་སྦྱར་ལ་དམིགས་པ་གཏད་ཅིང་། ཐུན་འཇོག་ཚེ་ལྟེ་བར་དམིགས་པ་གཏད་པ་སྤར་ཡོ་ དགའ་བ་འཁྱིལ་པ་བཞི་ནི་

Homage to the Guru Vajrayogini! Herein is the instruction that the Lord Narotapa did not give to others, but gave to the brothers, the Lords of Phamthing <note>Nepalese masters</note>. Among the deep knowledge of the Generation Stage and Completion Stage with their branches, the method for meditating on the eleven yogas of the Naropa tradition of Sky-Farer practice is as follows. Although Lord Naropa spoke of it first in the Indian texts and the "Immeasurables," in terms of the order of understanding and practice, it is thus: Sleeping, Rising, and Tasting Nectar; the Immeasurables, the Guru, and Arising as the Deity; Purifying Beings...

<leaf-break/>

...that is: if one sleeps in the state of the Generation Stage, one arises in the form of the Yogini without ornaments and hand-implements. One is prompted to rise by the sound of a <term>damaru</term> <gloss>small drum</gloss> in the sky and the resonance of the three <term>Om</term> mantra. According to the "Inconceivable" tradition, one rises as the Yogini in the manner of a fish jumping from water. Regarding "Tasting Nectar": put a nectar pill into liquor and taste it with the thought of offering it to the deity at the heart. Regarding the "Yoga of the Immeasurables": since it is complete within the generation of <term>bodhichitta</term>, it is not needed separately. Regarding the "Guru Yoga": visualize the Guru in the form of Vajradharma and pray... then, as for "Arising as the Deity": according to the general procedure, from the syllable <term>Bam</term> and the mantra garland, light radiates and fills the inside of the body, purifying sins and obscurations...

<leaf-break/>

...entering with the pride of having discarded the hand-implements. These practices of the Generation Stage explained thus are superior to others, because all the ripening and liberating instructions of the ultimate secret of yoga are contained herein. Furthermore, there are the four ripening empowerments, and they are contained here: the verbal recitation is introduced as the path of the Vase Empowerment; the mental recitation is introduced as the path of the Secret Empowerment; and the two higher empowerments are shown separately and introduced. The extensive path of the Vase Empowerment is the complete <term>Chakrasamvara</term>, and it is complete here: the "Source of Phenomena" <note>Dharmodayo</note> celestial palace of the extensive Generation Stage of the Father is symbolized by the two-tiered Source of Phenomena here. The moon inside it is the twenty-five Hero deities from the Blessed One up to Vajrasattva... the moon inside it is the twenty-five Hero deities from the Blessed One up to Vajrasattva. The fact that the seed syllables of the four elements are complete within the central <term>Bam</term> represents the four Heart Yoginis. The "bindu" <gloss>drop</gloss> of the <term>Bam</term> is the Venerable Lady. The mantra garland...

<leaf-break/>

The separate teaching of the two higher empowerments: visualize the Source of Phenomena with the <term>Bam</term> at the secret place. In the four corners, discarding the front and back of the Source of Phenomena, imagine the "Swirling of Joy" rotating and staying on the left. Apply the "union of winds" <note>breath control</note> and focus the visualization. At the time of ending the session, the focus is transferred to the navel. The four "Swirlings of Joy" are the four pure paths of Wisdom-Knowledge. The fact that each has four is the "fourteen purities." There are four for the Fourth Empowerment: since there are four paths that pervade the order of the four empowerments, the four Vase Empowerments are: one Source of Phenomena of "Swirling Joy" in the glory of visualizing oneself as the Yogini. One greyish-white "bindu" drop. Focus the mind on whichever is appropriate, or do it as a "taste-experience." By this, the non-conceptual meditative absorption is born. The second is: from the navel to the crown, the <term>Avadhuti</term> <gloss>central channel</gloss> is visualized with the <term>A-shad</term> <gloss>short-A stroke</gloss> pointing downwards. Visualize the <term>Bam</term> as the deity below. By the opening and closing of the "lower gate" <gloss>perineum</gloss>, the wind moves, the fire blazes and touches the <term>Bam</term>...

<summary>This page introduces the specialized Vajrayogini instructions of Naropa, focusing on the eleven yogas and the integration of the four empowerments into the Generation Stage practice. It explains the symbolic correspondence between the visualization elements and the tantric deities.</summary>
<keywords>Vajrayogini, Naropa, eleven yogas, Generation Stage, empowerments, Dharmodayo, Bam syllable, Phamthingpa</keywords>

གང་ལ་རེ་བ་བྱས་ཀྱང་རེ་བ་བཞིན་མི་འགྲུབ་པས་སྡུག་བསྔལ་བར་འགྱུར་པའི་རེ་དོང་སྤངས་ནས་རྩེ་གཅིག་ཏུ་བསྒྲུབ་པ་ལ་གཞོལ་བར་བྱ་སྟེ།ཇོ་བོ་ཆེན་པོས།འཇིག་རྟེན་བྱ་བ་དག་ལ་ཕར་བལྟས་པས།།བྱས་པ་ཐཾད་
དོན་མེད་སྡུག་བསྔལ་རྒྱུར།།ཅི་ལ་བསཾས་ཀྱང་སྙིང་པོ་མི་འདུག་པས།།རང་གི་སེམས་ལ་ལྟ་བ་བསྒོམ་པར་བགྱིས།།ཞེསོ།གཉིས་པ་དབེན་པར་གནས་ནས་ཚོང་དང་བུ་ལོན་སོང་(་་་)ནུར་ལ་བསོག་དུས་རྣཾས་སྤང་དགོསྟེ།
ཟང་ཟིང་ཕྱིར་ནི་རྩོད་གྱུར་ཅིང་།།ཟང་ཟིང་མེད་ན་བདེ་བའི་མཆོག།ཆུ་སྐྱར་གྱི(ས)་ནི་ཉ་རོ་དག།སྤངས་པས་བདེ་བ་ཐོབ་པར་གྱུར།།ཞེས་ཆུ་སྐྱར་ཞིགིས་ཉ་རོ་ཞིག་རྙེད་པ་ལ་ཆུ་སྐྱར་གཞན་རྣཾས་ཀྱིས་འདེད་ནས་འཕྲོག་
པས་ཤིན་ཏུ་སྡུག་བསྔལ་བར་གྱུར་པ་ལ།ཉ་རོ་དེ་བོར་བས་བདེ་བ་ཐོབ་པ་ལྟ་བུ་ཏེ།ཟང་ཟིང་གི་ནོར་ནི་འཚོལ་བའི་ཕྱིར་བདེ་སྡུག་གཏཾ་ངན་དུ་མ་ཁྱད་དུ་གསད་ནས་སྒྲུབ་དགོས་ཤིང་།ཅུང་ཟད་རྙེད་དུ་ཟིན་ཀྱང་སེར་

སྣང་དགེ་བའི་ལས་ཀྱིས་མ་གོས་པར་ཆོས་བརྒྱད་འཁྲི་བ་ཆོད་པའི་ཞེན་མེད་དྲག་པོས་དགོས་མེད་ཀྱི་བློ་སྣ་རྒྱུད་ལ་སྐྱེ་བ་ཞིག་དགོས་ཏེ། རྒྱལ་དབང་རྗེས། འཆི་བ་སྙིང་ཟུགི་དགོན་པ་ན།། འཇིག་རྟེན་བློས་བཏང་གི་སྒྲུབ་
པ་པོ།།འདོད་ཡོན་ཞེན་བཅད་ཀྱིས་མཚམས་བཅད་ནས།། སེཾས་ཆོས་བརྒྱད་ཀྱི་མི་དང་མཇལ་ཕྲད་མེད།། ཞེསོ། དེ་ལྟར་དབེན་པའི་གནས་སུ་ཉིས་ལེན་ལ་བརྩོན་ཁུལ་བྱས་ཀྱང་བསཾ་པ་ཁེ་འདོད་གྲཊ་འདོད་ལ་
སོཊ་པའི་བློ་ངན་དང་མ་འབྲལ་ན། ཕྱག་རྫོགས་སོཊ་མན་ངག་ཟབ་མོ་བསྒོམ་བློ་བྱས་ཀྱང་། ཉོན་མོང་པའི་གཉེན་པོར་འགྲོ་བར་དཀའ་སྟེ། ཁྲོ་ཕུ་ལོ་ཙ་བས། ཚེ་སྲོག་ལྦུ་བར་མ་ཤེས་ཤིང་།། ཞེ་ནས་འཆི་བ་མ་དྲན་ན།།
དགེ་ཕྱོཊ་མང་པོ་བྱས་འགྱུར་ཀྱང་།། ད་དུང་ཚེ་འདིའི་ལག་ཆ་ཡིན།། སྙན་གྲཊ་སྒྱུ་མར་མ་ཤེས་ཤིང་།། ཆེ་འདོད་ཁེ་གྲཊ་མ་བོར་ན།། མི་ཡི་དམ་པར་གཟུང་གྱུར་ཀྱང་།། ད་དུང་ཆོས་བརྒྱད་ཁོལ་པོ་ཡིན།། ཞེས་དང་།
རྒྱལ་སྲས་རིནོེས། དམ་ཆོས་ཐར་པའི་ལམ་དུ་འགྲོ་བ་ལ།། ཚེ་འདིའི་ཕུན་ཚོཊ་བསྒྲུབ་ལ་རྩེ་གཅིག་པའི།། བློ་ངན་འདི་ལས་བར་ཆད་ཆེ་བ་མེད།། དེ་ཕྱིར་རྣམ་པ་ཀུན་ཏུ་འདི་སྤངས་བྱ།། ཞེསོ། དེ་ན་རི་ཁྲོད་
འགྲིམས་པ་ལ་ཆང་སྡང་སྐྱེ་བའི་ཕ་ཡུལ་སྤངས།། ཞེན་ཆཊ་སྐྱེ་བའི་ནོར་རྫས་སྤངས།། ཉོན་མོངས་སྐྱེ་བའི་ཡུལ་ངན་སྤངས།། མི་འདོད་དུ་མ་སྐྱེ་ཞིང་བྱང་ཆུབ་སྒྲུབ་པ་ལ་གེཊ་བྱེད་པའི་ལྷ་བདུད་ཀྱིས་གཡབ་མོ་
ཉེ་འབྲེལ་སྤངས། ཆེ་འདོད་གྲཊ་འདོད་ཆོས་བརྒྱད་སྤངས། ཤུག་བསྔལ་ཐཾད་ཀྱི་རྩ་བ་འཁོར་བའི་ཁྱིམ་ཐབ་སྤངས། གཡེང་བའི་རྩ་བ་ངོ་བསྲུང་སྤངས། གྲོཊ་ངན་བྱུར་གྱི་གཉའ་ཤིང་སྤངས། མདོར་ན་ལ་ཁར་
འཆིན་བྱ་རོ་དང་། ཆུ་ཁར་ཤི་ན་ཉ་རོ་བཞིན་དུ་སུས་ཀྱང་བདག་ཏུ་གཟུང་བ་མེད་པ། གང་ལ་ཡང་མ་ཆཊ་པ། བསྡད་ན་ཕོང་རྗེས་དང་འགྲོ་ན་རྐང་རྗེས་ལས་མེད་པ། ཚེ་འདིའི་སྣང་ཤས་ཐཾད་ལིངས་ཀྱི་བསྐྱུར།

Likewise, whatever worldly or religious activities one hopes for, if they do not manifest as hoped, they become a pit of suffering. One should abandon such hopes and devote oneself one-pointedly to accomplishment. The Great Lord <note>Atisha Dipamkara</note> said:
Looking out at worldly activities,
Every action is a cause of meaningless suffering.
No matter what I think of, there is no essence,
So I shall practice looking into my own mind.

Second, while staying in solitude, one must abandon times of collecting debts, trading, or <unclear>...</unclear>.
For the sake of material things, conflict arises;
Without material things, there is supreme peace.
The heron, by abandoning
The fish carcass, attained happiness.
This refers to a heron that found a fish carcass and was chased and harassed by other herons trying to steal it, causing great suffering. By dropping the carcass, it attained peace. Similarly, material wealth must be sought by braving many hardships, bad reputations, and the mixture of pleasure and pain. Even if a little is found, one cannot enjoy it due to the power of stinginess; furthermore, there is the suffering of worrying about it being wasted, stolen by kings or thieves, and so forth. Because one accumulates many sins for the sake of wealth, one experiences many sufferings at the time of death. Since all these are undesirable, wealth should be abandoned. The Precious Bodhisattva <note>Gyalsay Thogme Zangpo</note> said:
While seeking it, one relies on a hundred afflictions.
When wanting to enjoy what is found, it is the basis of stinginess.
If stolen by others, it is the cause of lamentation.
What use is wealth that is useless after death?

Third, one must also abandon women, friends, and relatives. If they are not abandoned, one falls under the power of women and kin, and is diverted from accomplishing virtue.
The undertakings of a household are suffering;
They never lead to happiness.
The snake, seeing the dwelling of another,
Entered it and attained happiness.
This refers to a snake that was being bothered by its own young in its nest; by going to another place, it attained peace. Correspondingly, one must abandon "beloved villages" because they interrupt the accomplishment of Dharma. The Precious Bodhisattva said:
If they are present before you,

<leaf-break/>

it is like that. Even if one stays in solitude with many companions, it is a basis for the increase of heedless idle talk. Therefore, it is important to stay alone like a mountain or a wounded deer. <term>Bara-ba</term> said:
If one or two gather, there is talk.
If many gather, it is the cause of attachment, hatred, and dispute.
Since it is difficult to overcome a harsh and formidable environment,
Stay alone; it arises from the strength of virtue.

Furthermore, one must not be stained by "apparent virtuous activities" such as building projects or festivals under the name of "pure virtue" in solitude. One needs a strong lack of attachment that cuts the ties to the <term>eight worldly concerns</term> <gloss>hope for gain and fear of loss, hope for pleasure and fear of pain, hope for fame and fear of insignificance, hope for praise and fear of blame</gloss>, so that the thought of "no need" arises in the mind-stream. <term>Gyalwang Je</term> said:
In the hermitage where death pierces the heart,
The practitioner who has mentally abandoned the world
Has closed the boundary by cutting attachment to sensory pleasures.
The mind does not meet the people of the eight worldly concerns.

Thus, even if one claims to be diligent in practice in a solitary place, if one is not separated from the evil mind of wanting profit, fame, and so on, then even if one tries to meditate on the profound instructions of <term>Mahamudra</term> or <term>Dzogchen</term>, it will be difficult for it to serve as an antidote to the afflictions. <term>Thropu Lotsawa</term> said:
If you do not realize that life is like a bubble,
And do not remember death from your heart,
Though you perform many virtuous acts,
They are still just tools for this life.
If you do not realize fame is like an illusion,
And do not cast away the desire for greatness, profit, and renown,
Though you be held as a supreme person,
You are still a slave to the eight worldly concerns.

And the Precious Bodhisattva said:
For the path to liberation through the sacred Dharma,
There is no greater obstacle than this evil mind
Which is one-pointedly focused on accomplishing the excellence of this life.
Therefore, abandon this in every way.

Thus, when roaming mountain retreats, abandon the homeland where attachment and hatred arise. Abandon wealth and possessions where clinging arises. Abandon bad environments where afflictions arise. Abandon relatives who act as "divine demons" <note>temptations that look like help</note> beckoning you and obstructing the accomplishment of enlightenment. Abandon the eight worldly concerns of wanting greatness and fame. Abandon the household life, the root of all suffering. Abandon "saving face," the root of distraction. Abandon bad companions, the yoke of misfortune. In short, be like a bird's corpse on a mountain pass or a fish's corpse on a riverbank, claimed by no one, attached to nothing. When staying, leave no trace but the mark of your bottom; when going, leave no trace but your footprints. Completely cast away all appearances of this life.

...having seen, renunciation is born from the depths, like a person with a vomiting sickness who has lost all craving for food. Among the beings of the six realms, there is not a single one who has not been one's own mother, having raised us with kindness since beginningless time. Because they have cared for us with kindness just like our mother in this life, we must train in the common path, such as learning the two types of Bodhicitta—aspiration and application—which seek perfect enlightenment for the sake of sentient beings, thereby purifying the continuum to become a fit vessel. As the Lord of Conquerors, Lapa, said: "If the continuum is not purified by the common path, riding an unsubdued elephant will bring about one's own ruin." Just so, a person like a jewel is required to enter the path of Mantra. First, one must strive until the marrow of the bones is reached in the practice of the stages of the path to enlightenment, which identifies the nature of non-conceptuality. The common preliminaries should be known in detail from other sources.

Second, regarding the specific preliminaries: Having purified the continuum through the common ones, in order to enter the Vajra Vehicle of Secret Mantra, first one must receive the general unsurpassed empowerments and specifically the profound Body Mandala of the "Tibetan-faced" <term>Chakrasamvara</term> from a Guru who is like the Lord of the Mandala, under whom the wisdom of empowerment can truly be born in the disciple's continuum and the transfer of blessings can occur. By the stages of the four empowerments of the definitive meaning, the three doors, which have dwelt primordially as the three bodies of the deity, are purified of the temporary stains of the mind along with their habitual tendencies. Empowerments that certainly plant the seeds of the four bodies in the disciple's continuum must be properly bestowed. 

For the Vase Empowerment, the basis of purification is the five aggregates. By bestowing the empowerment of the five families, which are the purifiers, the result of purification is that the five aggregates appear as the five families, the four elements as the four Mothers, and the elements and sense bases as the mandala of the male and female Bodhisattvas. Thus, one is authorized to meditate on the Generation Stage, which is like an illusory light-body of purified appearances, and the Vajra Body of the <term>Nirmanakaya</term> <gloss>Emanation Body</gloss> will be quickly accomplished. Through the outer refuge, the obscurations of the three doors are purified, and the blessings of the Three Jewels enter the continuum, causing experience and realization to quickly arise. Through the inner refuge, the births, deaths, and the intermediate state are transformed into the Body, Speech, and Mind of the Conquerors; through the quick arising of the realization of the first stage <note>Generation Stage</note> in the continuum, it becomes a maturing factor. Through the secret refuge, the realization of the completion stage, the <term>Mahamudra</term> <gloss>Great Seal</gloss> of bliss and emptiness, is matured into liberation. These and other unique oral lineages of refuge, the hundred syllables, the mandala, and the Guru Yoga—the oral instructions that distinguish each of these into outer, inner, and secret—should be learned from the Guru's own mouth. They can also be known from the previously composed manual, the *Stream of Nectar*.

Second, resolving through the View: All phenomena included within appearance and existence, samsara and nirvana, are the unceasing dawning of one's own mind. In relation to the mind that is clear while appearing, they are the relative truth. Because the mind, the object of appearance, is not established as any essence or nature whatsoever, from the side of its emptiness, it is established as the absolute truth. As said in the *Buddhapalita*: "The Buddhas' teaching of the Dharma is perfectly based on the two truths: the world's relative truth and the truth of the ultimate meaning." 

The relative is also two-fold: the false relative and the authentic relative. First, the false relative is: the mind is corrupted by the habitual tendencies of ignorance, and though it does not exist in essence, it is the impurity of delusive appearances. It is this being wounded by the suffering of subject-object grasping and pleasure-pain, appearing as the various phenomena of samsara included within the container and its contents <note>the world and its beings</note>. Like a sword-spinner cutting wood, cut through the wandering mind and place the mind firmly on the focal point. As Padampa Sangye said: "If it wanders, cut the root. If it is agitated, rest it in the expanse." Furthermore, when agitation occurs, by looking at the essence of the place of wandering, the one who wanders, and the act of wandering, they are not established anywhere, and the characteristics will be naturally liberated in their own place. Lord Milarepa said: "When the mind is agitated, trample it with the gaze. How wonderful is this natural liberation of the mind's characteristics!" And from the Sutras: "It is taught as very important to hold the mind by meditating on impermanence and the suffering of Samsara." 

Dullness and agitation are the primary obstacles to accomplishing Calm Abiding. One must also certainly recognize and abandon regret, lethargy, sleep, and doubt. Regret is when one dwells on some past action, whether appropriate or not, and by vividly remembering whether it was right or wrong, the mind is not allowed to rest. Lethargy is a state of delusion where both body and mind are heavy and inflexible. Sleep occurs when one relies on the causes of sleep and the senses that engage with objects are withdrawn, causing the focal point to waver. Doubt is when one wonders whether Calm Abiding will be accomplished or not, and thus does not wish to engage with the focal point. Furthermore, craving for external desirable things and malice toward others are also obstacles to accomplishing Calm Abiding and Special Insight. 

As an antidote to these, the Precious One of Oddiyana said: "If lethargic, pray to the Guru, rouse the awareness, and meditate using methods to gladden the mind. If the mind drifts, tighten with discipline. Gather it completely. Cast the gaze to the tip of the nose..." 

<leaf-break/>

If you sustain the state as a continuous flow, realization will certainly dawn. All focal points and signs are completely transcended. O Yogi, always rest in evenness! 

By binding the mind in one-pointed concentration, problems like wind being blocked in the upper body, aching of the eye sockets, fainting without cause, and sharp pains are very likely to occur. Whatever happens, abandon thoughts of the past and future. Without trying to fix or alter the present awareness, sustain the mindfulness of recognizing your own nature within the vivid, clear, natural state, and rest in evenness. 

From the *Great Perfection: Total Space*: "Do not analyze the past; discard perceptions of what has gone. Do not anticipate the future; cut the mind's tether of expectation. In the middle, rest in the state of the sky, without grasping." 

By resting in that way, all the ways thoughts arise will become naturally pure and naturally liberated, becoming equal in the state of vivid clarity. Therefore, it is also called the "Yoga of Equal Taste." 

Within this state of vivid clarity, without any attachment or desire—such as thinking about whether to meditate or not, being happy if the mind stays, or unhappy if it wanders—relax loosely into a state where the mind is spacious and wide awake. Without the contrivance of stopping or establishing anything, let the mind settle in its natural state. On top of that, you must sustain the seal of vivid mindfulness without wandering. 

The analogy is like untying the rope of a tethered calf. When a herder tethers a calf to a stake, it feels confined and, instead of eating grass, it pulls this way and that. When it is untied and allowed to drink, it follows the mother and then, feeling relaxed, it settles down and eats grass. Similarly, if you over-tighten the "grip" of mindfulness, the mind becomes agitated and will not stay. Therefore, do not think of anything except for a mere vigilant observation of non-wandering. Relax loosely. You must let it rest in spaciousness. 

The Great Brahmin Saraha said: "Those who are bound attempt to go in the ten directions. When released, they remain unmoving..."

<summary>This page discusses managing obstacles like physical pain and mental wandering during meditation. It uses the "Equal Taste" and "Sky-like" metaphors to describe the natural state of mind beyond past and future thoughts.</summary>

—one should ensure that the meaning of the non-existent is not lost. Through conduct that embraces hardship, in a place without enemies or friends, dwelling alone like a beggar or a rhinoceros, being content with poor food and clothing, one should practice one-pointedness. Then, having purified oneself as a suitable vessel through common and uncommon preliminaries, if one focuses on the Great Perfection, one should turn back attachment to the body, speech, and mind through the conduct of "separating cyclic existence and transcendence" <note>original: "ru shan"</note>. Through "conduct like a mute," cut off speech. Through "conduct like a small child," leave the mind unaltered and relaxed, and do not be separated from the meaning of the Dharma-nature. Through the conduct of "taking the path onto the vow," whatever conditions arise must be taken as the path to forcibly cut the mind's clinging. Lord Thatsapa said: "Sickness, suffering, and bad conditions are indispensable for purifying previous karma. The results of karma are not lost by avoiding them; recognize the nature of the one who is sick." Through "conduct like a dog or a pig," where there is no clean or dirty, abandon the attachment to acceptance and rejection. Through the "conduct of a madman," where things happen spontaneously and unceasingly, take whatever appears onto the path without acceptance or rejection. As it is said: "With conduct like a bee, taste the flavor of all phenomena. With conduct like a rhinoceros, completely abandon the objects that cause confusion. With conduct like a mute, cut off the speech of all cleverness. With conduct like a pigeon, abandon doubt regarding the Secret Mantra. With conduct like a madman, abandon dwelling in single places. With conduct like a lion, abandon a fearful mind and roam in charnel grounds. With conduct like a dog or a pig, abandon the objects of purity and conceptualization." One should train in such behaviors without reversing the order. Furthermore, one should abandon like poison the wrong behaviors such as "mouthing the view" <note>talking about realization without having it</note>, reckless conduct, and pretending to be liberated while unliberated. Since the enhancement of meditation is devotion, be persistent in Guru Yoga and supplication. Since the master of meditation is the turning away of attachment, completely—

—by meditating for a long duration, meditative concentration arises in which the essence of awareness is clear and sustained along with experiences of bliss. From the time it is slightly difficult to sustain until the meditation becomes continuous, this is "Small One-Pointedness." When the meditative concentration appears even when one is not meditating, and one has gained mastery such that it is stable when one does meditate, this is "Middling One-Pointedness." When the meditative concentration appears unceasingly, such that formal meditation and post-meditation merge and one moves entirely within the state of sustaining clear awareness, this is "Great One-Pointedness." When one realizes the essence of the mind is free from arising, ceasing, and elaboration, but is not separated from the experience of "grasping at emptiness," and has hopes of wanting to abandon cyclic existence and achieve Nirvana, this is "Small Freedom from Elaboration." When even the grasping at emptiness is purified, but grasping at hopes and fears regarding outer appearances still occurs and doubts are not resolved, this is "Middling Freedom from Elaboration." When grasping at emptiness is liberated regarding all phenomena included within appearance and existence, cyclic existence and transcendence, and one is free from hope and fear and doubts are resolved, this is "Great Freedom from Elaboration." When one realizes all phenomena as the essence of the union of the Great Seal, but still has a lingering sense of experience and grasping conviction, this is "Small One-Taste." When the grasping conviction of many things as one taste is purified, so that the appearance of outer objects does not remain as separate, and the mind that grasps at them does not remain as internal, but appearance and mind are mixed as indivisible, this is "Middling One-Taste." When one realizes all of appearance and existence as many things of one taste, and that thought of one taste arises as the appearance of the many, thus subsiding into the natural state, this is "Great One-Taste." When appearances arise as meditation without needing to be held by mindfulness or needing to intentionally rest in equanimity, so there is no distinction between the object and subject of meditation, but a slight experience of "grasping at illusion" arises, this is "Small Non-Meditation." By dissolving into the heart-life-force, think that the obscurations of the mind are purified and the body is purified as the deity’s body. Rotate this three times while maintaining devotion, and at the end of the nine-fold gentle breathing, exhale three times forcefully and equally. Think that the twenty-one thousand equal portions of the three poisons are expelled, and the ground for the re-arising of afflictions is emptied. In return, all the inexhaustible blessing-power of the Buddhas and their heirs' three secrets of body, speech, and mind is obtained by oneself, purifying the sins and obscurations of the three gates. One develops the conviction of the play of the three <term>kayas</term> <gloss>Buddha bodies</gloss>. Then, visualize yourself as <term>Heruka</term>. At the throat, the wheel of enjoyment <gloss>throat chakra</gloss>, the syllable <term>AH</term>—the essence of the sixty aspects of the melodic speech of all Buddhas—blazes like a sun. Its flames burn away the physical tongue into nothingness. In its place, a red eight-petaled lotus clearly appears. In its center, on a sun disk, is a red syllable <term>AH</term> with the radiance of a hundred thousand suns, bubbling up like water from water.
<leaf-break/>
Think of white syllables like a crystal rosary, coming forth beyond reach and dissolving into the <term>AH</term> on the tongue, and imagine that all the blessings of the Buddha’s body are acquired under your own power. Again, immeasurable light rays radiate, inviting all the blessing-power of the sixty aspects of the melodic speech of the Buddhas and their heirs, as well as the power of the speech of gods and humans who have achieved truthful speech, in the form of red consonants. By their dissolving, think that you gain mastery over the qualities of the Buddha's speech. Again, rays radiate, and all the qualities of the Buddhas' and their heirs' heart—knowledge, love, and power—arrive in the form of blue <term>ye dharma</term> syllables. By their dissolving, imagine that you obtain mastery over the qualities of the Buddha's heart. Again, rays radiate to the Buddhas and heirs, and especially from the summit of Mount Meru, the entire assembly of deities of the <term>Chakrasamvara</term> mandala, both the support and the supported, are invited in the form of the essence mantras.
<leaf-break/>
These majestic ones, and especially the qualities that are high upon the crowns of the great beings of the Brahma realm; the power of Ishvara; the wealth of Indra; the intellectual strength of Vishnu; beautiful forms like the bodies of the gods; sweet speech like that of the daughters of the Gandharvas; the material wealth of Nanda, Upananda, and Takshaka; the dominion of Jambhala and Vaishravana; all the desired splendors of the five sensory qualities of a universal monarch—everything that exists as desired is summoned in the form of the seven royal possessions and so forth. Gather them all together and think that they dissolve into the syllable <term>AH</term>. Then again, light radiates from the <term>AH</term>, striking the mantra garlands of vowels and consonants. The vowels from <term>OM</term> onwards gradually dissolve into the <term>AH</term>. Similarly, the consonants and <term>ye dharma</term> dissolve into the heart-life-force, and finally they all dissolve into the <term>AH</term>. That <term>AH</term> syllable also dissolves into the sun seat. The sun seat dissolves into the lotus. The lotus dissolves into light.

It arises suddenly like light. That is inseparable from the upward-moving wind and inseparable from one's own mind. From that, on the edge of the sun seat, the white vowels emerge in sequence, circling clockwise once. Similarly, the red consonants circle once. Inside that, the blue <term>ye dharma</term> circles once. Inside that, the essence mantra of the <term>Yidam</term>, white with a slight red tint, circles. Imagine they are as fine and clear as if drawn with the tip of a hair, radiating immeasurable light, having the nature of the five wisdoms of empty-clarity. Recite from the mouth the vowels, consonants, and <term>ye dharma</term> with the three qualities of being clear, distinct, and audible. Light rays of their respective colors radiate from them. Especially from the central <term>AH</term> syllable, infinite and boundless light rays radiate, inviting all the blessings of the bodies of the Buddhas and their heirs abiding in the lands of the ten directions—the thirty-two marks and eighty signs.
<leaf-break/>
By dissolving into the <term>AH</term> syllable, think that you have the quality of being able to purify the sins and downfalls of the bodies of beings just by seeing the Buddha’s body, and the quality of being able to transform the appearance of wrong views; the quality of being able to turn the wheel of the profound and vast Dharma according to each being's disposition just by hearing the speech; the quality of being able to purify the sins and downfalls of the mind just by remembering the heart, leading beings to the higher realms and the certain good <gloss>liberation</gloss>; and especially, think that you have gained mastery over the blessing-power that ensures the accomplishment of the supreme <term>mahamudra</term> <gloss>great seal</gloss> siddhi in this very life. Again, as the light strikes the environment and its inhabitants, the essence of the four elements of the outer world is summoned uncontrollably in the form of the eight auspicious symbols, large and small spheres of light, and wish-fulfilling jewels. Like a magnet attracting iron filings, they all dissolve into the syllable <term>A</term>. Again, the light radiates, and the life-force, merit, power, fame, wealth, splendor, and majesty of the sentient beings who are the inhabitants—
<leaf-break/>
are dissolved into light. The tongue becomes a one-pointed vajra with a tube of light. Inside the tube, the <term>AH</term> syllable is stirred by the breath, and you think it proclaims the sound of the mantra. This completes the blessing of speech. Regarding the difficulty of finding the freedoms and advantages: the text says "difficult to find and of great meaning." The difficulty of finding is explained through three ways: example, cause, and number. The example is like a blind turtle putting its neck into the hole of a golden yoke floating in the ocean. The golden yoke is heavy and tends to sink, yet it floats on the surface of the water; the turtle has a short neck and the ocean is vast. Although it is impossible for the two to meet, it happens by sheer chance. Similarly, obtaining this precious support of the freedoms and advantages at this time is difficult to find according to the example. Regarding the difficulty of finding by way of number: beings in the hells are as numerous as the dust of the earth; <term>pretas</term> <gloss>hungry ghosts</gloss> are as numerous as snowflakes; animals are as numerous as the dregs of wine. On top of that, he holds an alms bowl of blue lapis lazuli. At his brow, a white <term>HAM</term> is clearly visualized, from which a stream of white, undefiled nectar of the nature of <term>bodhichitta</term> descends, filling the alms bowl to the brim. Inside it, from the syllable <term>PAM</term>, a twenty-five tiered lotus stalk grows. On a portion of its thirteen petals, this world of endurance <term>Saha</term>, its formation and so forth, are visualized in detail as in the <term>Abhidharmakosha</term> and the separate extensive mandala rituals. Furthermore, there are the outer offerings: forms, sounds, smells, tastes, and so forth; the inner offerings: white and red <term>bodhichitta</term> and so forth; the secret offerings: the materials of the <term>tsog</term> <gloss>feast gathering</gloss> to be enjoyed, the five meats, five nectars, and so forth. Finally, enjoying the flavor with the non-dual wisdom of bliss and emptiness, one rests in the state of <term>mahamudra</term>, the natural mode free from the concepts of what is offered and the one who offers. To explain it slightly more extensively: from the non-wavering state of self-awareness, bliss and emptiness itself, the unobstructed creative power of awareness manifests as sixteen-year-old offering goddesses—
<leaf-break/>
Together with many, they dissolve into the consort of the object of offering. All the objects of offering, such as the father and mother deities, are pleased by the offering of bliss and emptiness and enter into union. The stream of white and red <term>bodhichitta</term> descends, which is then again enjoyed in the reverse order of the levels. The feast substances are various foods and drinks of gods and humans, regardless of being clean or dirty, sweet or bitter, which are blessed as being of the nature of the five meats and five nectars and then offered. These also exist on each of the twenty-five tiers of the lotus stalk, each having a thousand petals. On each petal, there are an uncountable number of three-thousandfold world systems. In each three-thousandfold system, one should visualize and offer inconceivable and unimaginable offering goddesses. Then, the offering substances, which are none other than self-awareness, such as the Vairocana in front, melt into light and are gathered into the syllable <term>HUM</term>, dissolving into the heart as before. The assemblies of deities of <term>Heruka</term>, who are the objects of offering—
<leaf-break/>
A triangular source of phenomena <gloss>dharmodaya</gloss>, white on the outside and red on the inside. The base is narrow and points downward; the top is wide and points upward. Inside it, upon a sun and moon seat, is a white syllable <term>HUM</term>, sparkling and bright, clear and pure. From it, light radiates, and all the blessings and power of the body, speech, and mind of the Buddhas and their heirs dissolve into the <term>HUM</term>. Again, light radiates, purifying the ordinary appearances and attachments of the environment and inhabitants, blessing them as the play of the three <term>kayas</term>' wisdom. The light rays gather back, and the <term>HUM</term> syllable transforms into the Bhagavan with the donkey face <note>this refers to the Donkey-Faced Heruka, a specific form of Chakrasamvara</note>. He is white, with one face, four arms, and three eyes. His first two hands hold a vajra and bell; the lower two hold a <term>khatvanga</term> <gloss>ritual staff</gloss> and a trident. With his right leg extended, he treads upon the crown of the black <term>Bhairava</term>, who lies face down. With his left leg slightly bent, he treads upon the navel of the red <term>Kalaratri</term>. His hair is bound three times with the thread of Brahma, and at its peak is a jewel top—
